title: American Muslims Fight Stereotypes

image.attribution: U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) / Wikimedia Commons / Public Domain.

main_content:
Muslims around the world will celebrate the holiday of Eid-al-Fitr, the end of the holy month of Ramadan. Ramadan is a time when Muslims fast and focus on God.

For Muslims in the United States, it is also a time to reflect and fight negative stereotypes of Islam. Muslims feel Islamic extremists hurt their community.

Ahsan Mahmood Khan is the President of the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community Los Angeles East Chapter. He says the news does not reflect who Muslims are.

“You hear a lot in the news about (the Islamic State group) ISIL or ISIS and what is going on in the Middle East. It is just terrible, and we hear this in the news every day.”

Mohammed Zafarullah is the imam of the Baitul Hammed Mosque. He says Islam is a religion of peace. But extremism has led to misconceptions about Islam.

A 2011 study showed that Muslims in the U.S. are concerned about the acts of Islamic extremists. The study explains how life became more difficult for Muslim-Americans after the September 11 attacks. Some Muslims reported that people looked at them with suspicion and called them offensive names.

questions.question: What does the holiday Eid-al-Fitr mark?
options: The end of the holy month of Ramadan
A celebration of peace and tolerance
A time for Muslims to gather in prayer
questions.answer: The end of the holy month of Ramadan

questions.question: What did imam Mohammed Zafarullah say about Islam?
options: It is frequently misunderstood due to extremists
It is only practiced by a minority of people
It requires fasting throughout the year
questions.answer: It is frequently misunderstood due to extremists

questions.question: What did some Muslims report?
options: Increased acceptance and understanding from the community
Feeling respected and valued after September 11
Experiencing suspicion and name-calling after September 11
A decrease in participation in public events
questions.answer: Experiencing suspicion and name-calling after September 11
